extracted.intended_audience: general readers, scholars of humor/media, comedians and media producers interested in humor about traumatic events
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for producing or evaluating humor that references the September 11 attacks, covering stage, print, broadcast, advertising and online memes, and how audiences and institutions responded. Useful for creators deciding whether and how to joke about 9/11 and for analysts studying cultural reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / 'Too soon!'
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience reaction that jokes told in the immediate wake of tragedies are often rejected as 'too soon'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gilbert Gottfried's 9/11 gag 18 days after the attacks provoked gasps, boos and a 'Too soon!' shout; late-night comedy and humorous publications avoided material for several weeks after 9/11. Use temporal distance as a factor when deciding whether to present material about the attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a point or express feelings (vs. gratuitous punching-at-victims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor about 9/11 should either make a point or express something people were feeling rather than directly poking fun at the loss of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Onion's post-9/11 issue avoided jokes that 'directly poked fun at the loss of life' and instead produced pieces intended to 'make a point or express something people were feeling.' Creators should prefer commentary/processing over mockery of victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional appropriateness / taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a joke is in 'bad taste' or 'poor taste' given its subject matter and audience sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of condemnation: Joan Rivers' 2002 joke about widows received official rebuke from the International Association of Fire Fighters; Miracle Mattress withdrew an ad themed around the Twin Towers after intense public criticism. Evaluate jokes for potential offense to victims, families, and broader communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reaction and institutional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of how specific audiences, broadcasters, publishers, or institutions will react, and whether content meets their standards and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family Guy's 9/11 material 'squeaked past the Fox standards and practices department' and provoked media commentary; stage roasts, TV networks, and publishers differ in tolerance. Anticipate boos, backlash, censorship, or acceptance depending on venue and gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium/context sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptability and form of 9/11 humor vary by medium — on stage, on screen, in print, in advertising, and online (memes/videos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Onion cancelled and then published a special print issue; comedians addressed the attacks onstage with mixed reactions; an advertising campaign (Miracle Mattress) was quickly pulled; online memes and viral videos spread widely. Tailor content to the norms and affordances of the chosen medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical framing and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the joke is framed as satire/commentary (e.g., social or political point) rather than as mere shock or tasteless provocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Onion's coverage aimed to comment on public feeling; South Park and Family Guy episodes often used satirical frames to address conspiracy theories or cultural reactions. Satirical framing can increase acceptability if it clearly targets ideas, institutions, or shared feelings rather than victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of humor (coping/constructing response to trauma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that humor can serve social and psychological functions after a disaster, such as helping people cope, process trauma, or construct collective response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (Bill Ellis, Giselinde Kuipers) found jokes began quickly after the attacks and served functions in public discourse. When evaluating such humor, consider whether it aids processing or merely exploits tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical distance and changing acceptability over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptability of 9/11 jokes can change with time; material that was unacceptable immediately after the attacks may become more tolerated later, and norms evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early immediate rejection contrasted with later television episodes and comedy specials that incorporated 9/11 references; 20th-anniversary charity events involved 9/11-related comedy. Consider historical moment and shifting public attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational and commercial risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential for commercial backlash, boycotts, and reputational harm if content is perceived as offensive or exploitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miracle Mattress's 'Twin Towers, Twin Price' ad provoked calls for boycotts and forced the company to pull the ad and close a location temporarily. Creators and advertisers should weigh brand risk and likely consumer reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to victims, families, and affected professions
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account the direct human cost and how jokes might affect survivors, families of victims, and professions (e.g., firefighters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joan Rivers' joke drew condemnation from the International Association of Fire Fighters; Pete Davidson's routines are informed by his personal loss. Consider proximity of the comedian/creator to victims and the potential harm to affected communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of conspiracy theories and misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: How humor engages with 9/11-related conspiracy theories — whether it lampoons them or unintentionally amplifies misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes internet memes lampooning conspiracy theories ('Bush did 9/11', 'jet fuel can't melt steel beams'). Satire that clearly mocks conspiracism can deflate it, but creators should avoid reproducing false claims without clear critical framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/award considerations and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators and publishers may edit or remove 9/11-related content to improve award chances or avoid controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 9/11 joke was cut from Jean Dujardin's film The Players reportedly to 'improve the chance of an Oscar award.' Producers should be aware that awards bodies, distributors, and festivals may be sensitive to such content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cultural and geographic sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cultures and countries may view references to traumatic historical events differently; what is acceptable in one place may be offensive in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Japanese Twitter users made 9/11/Barbenheimer memes; discussion notes Oppenheimer's sensitivity in Japan due to atomic-bomb history. Consider international audiences and local historical sensitivities when creating or distributing material.
